name: Cicero
role: Roman statesman, lawyer, orator and philosopher (106-43 BCE)
summary: Roman senator and consul who defended the Republic against Catiline, Caesar and Antony, and argued in the Republic and De Officiis for a mixed constitution under natural law, secure private property, active civic duty and the authority of the Senate. He opposed agrarian redistribution and debt cancellation and honoured tyrannicide, while holding that rule by the mere multitude is no true commonwealth.

notes: Read from local Gutenberg copies and a library copy of De Officiis, searched by theme: constitution, democracy, monarchy and tyranny, natural law, property and debt, agrarian laws, welfare/grain, war and empire, religion and auspices, succession of kings, family, duties, civic participation, tyrannicide. De Officiis dialogue positions are the speakers' (Scipio, Laelius) as presented by Cicero; the Republic survives in fragments. The IEP does not treat property, slavery or empire. De Legibus is not in the local corpus. Most modern statements (welfare state, gender, drugs, technology, international organisations) concern matters Cicero never addressed and are null.
